modules.name: Capital Allocation
modules.guidance: Use the management-commentary / conference-call data to understand where management is allocating capital among the five uses below, and how that allocation is behaving over time.

parameters.name: Capex for growth (not maintenance)
parameters.signal: High and rising GROWTH capex with high incremental ROIC; not just maintenance.
parameters.description: Distinguish growth capex from maintenance capex. Growth capex should be the maximum share, and the potential ROIC from the new growth capex should be high and good.
cautions: Do not confuse maintenance capex with growth capex

parameters.name: Advertisement and promotion
parameters.signal: A&P spend that durably builds brand equity and drives sales, judged like capex.
parameters.description: Marketing spend that creates brand and increases sales. Though not classified as capex, it ideally IS a capital expenditure and should be judged as one.
cautions: Reported as opex but should be assessed as brand-building capital

parameters.name: Research and development
parameters.signal: R&D that consistently yields new products/customers; high long-term R&D efficiency.
parameters.description: R&D that helps new product creation and new customer acquisition. Determine the long-term R&D efficiency (output per unit of R&D over time).

parameters.name: Merger and acquisition
parameters.signal: Small, simple, complementary bolt-ons; acquiree already strong; post-deal OPM improves.
parameters.description: Acquisitions are a common source of value destruction. Small bolt-on acquisitions have a higher chance of succeeding. The rare, valuable skill is systematically improving operations of the acquired business — one common parameter is OPM improvement after the acquisition. Prefer buying businesses that are already strong, and small/simple/complementary deals.
cautions: Big transformational M&A destroys value; large inorganic bets are a red flag

parameters.name: Distribution to shareholders
parameters.signal: Buybacks executed at low valuations; a coherent, disciplined distribution policy.
parameters.description: Dividends and buybacks. The best companies buy back stock advantageously (when cheap), but in practice buybacks mostly happen at elevated valuations.
cautions: Most buybacks occur at elevated valuations and destroy value

parameters.name: Cost of working capital
parameters.signal: Low or negative working capital; short / improving cash conversion cycle.
parameters.description: Money stuck in working capital leads to lower return on capital. Prefer businesses with low or negative working capital (rare).
cautions: Low/negative working-capital businesses are rare

parameters.name: Return on capital (headline)
parameters.signal: High and durable CROCI / return on capital, adjusted for goodwill.
parameters.description: Return on capital depends on asset turns and profit margin. The better metric is Cash Return on Cash Capital Invested (CROCI) = post-tax cash return / capital invested after adjusting accounting conventions such as goodwill.
cautions: Adjust capital for accounting conventions (e.g. goodwill) before judging

parameters.name: Asset turn
parameters.signal: High asset turnover (asset-light) COMBINED with a protecting moat.
parameters.description: A measure of asset intensity. Asset-light industries are attractive, but they must also carry additional competitive advantages to protect returns.
cautions: Asset-light alone is not enough; needs an additional competitive advantage

parameters.name: Profit margin
parameters.signal: High gross margin (pricing power) + high, STABLE operating margin (moat).
parameters.description: Higher gross margins show pricing power. High operating margin together with high gross margin indicates competitive advantage. Big swings in OPM indicate major cost components that are not in management's control.
cautions: Large OPM swings => key costs outside management control (a red flag)

parameters.name: Gain in market share
parameters.signal: Runway to gain share (not already dominant); evidence of share capture.
parameters.description: Growth from taking share. Share gains are easier in the early years; a company already above ~50% market share will find further gains tough.
cautions: >50% share makes further share gains hard

parameters.name: Geographical expansion
parameters.signal: Credible, well-executed geographic expansion; premium brand that travels well.
parameters.description: Growth by entering new geographies. Challenging, but powerful if implemented well. Premium brands transition to new markets more easily.
cautions: Geographic expansion is challenging and often poorly executed

parameters.name: Pricing, Mix and Volume
parameters.signal: Growth led by PRICING and MIX rather than volume.
parameters.description: The three ways to grow revenue. (1) Pricing power - raise prices without a rise in cost; customers price-insensitive (brands, status, luxury) - most valuable. (2) Mix optimisation - shift toward higher value-added products - highly valuable. (3) Volume growth - least valuable; total costs (incl. working capital) rise with volume.
cautions: Volume-led growth is the least valuable; costs scale with it

parameters.name: Cyclical market growth
parameters.signal: Positioned near the bottom of a cycle with an identifiable upturn ahead.
parameters.description: A double-edged sword. Investment aligned with a cyclical uptrend can give bumper returns; the way to invest is usually at the BOTTOM of the cycle. Endeavour to understand cycles to ride the upside and avoid the downside.
cautions: Do not extrapolate a cyclical uptrend as structural (a common mistake)

parameters.name: Structural end-market growth
parameters.signal: End market in permanent secular expansion.
parameters.description: Permanent expansion in the end market - the highest-quality growth.
cautions: Do not mistake a cyclical uptrend for structural growth

parameters.name: Persistence of growth
parameters.signal: Consistent, predictable ~10-15% growth; high CFROI supporting future growth.
parameters.description: There is no relation between the growth of the previous 5 years and the next 5 years. Find the subset of companies that keep generating consistent and predictable growth (10-15% range). The link is return on capital: higher CFROI usually means higher future earnings growth (more internal accruals to deploy).
cautions: Past 5-yr growth does NOT predict next 5-yr growth; look for consistency + ROC

parameters.name: Disciplined stewards
parameters.signal: Organic focus; prudent leverage; counter-cyclical investment; no big M&A.
parameters.description: Management with the patience and discipline to invest in organic growth, run a prudent balance sheet, and invest counter-cyclically, with big inorganic bets absent.
cautions: Big inorganic bets are a discipline red flag

parameters.name: Independent, long-term and tenacious
parameters.signal: Evidence of long-term vision executed with independence and tenacity.
parameters.description: Independent-minded, long-term-oriented, tenacious management that eradicates threats and stays the course on a long-term vision.

parameters.name: Out of limelight
parameters.signal: Low-profile, substance-over-celebrity management.
parameters.description: Prefer management that stays out of the limelight. Award-winning celebrity CEOs tend to underperform relative to their own prior record and to peers.
cautions: Award-winning CEOs underperform vs their prior record and vs peers

parameters.name: People matter (talent development)
parameters.signal: Systematic talent development; strong internal leadership pipeline.
parameters.description: Management that recognises developing talent as a top priority.

parameters.name: Candor
parameters.signal: Clear, candid communication of priorities and rationale; owns mistakes.
parameters.description: Effective, candid communication to investors about what matters and why.

parameters.name: Halo effect (caution)
parameters.signal: Assessment that is robust to the halo effect (separates results from skill).
parameters.description: A note of caution: much of our thinking about management is shaped by the halo effect (good results make us over-attribute skill). Guard against it.
cautions: Much management judgement is distorted by the halo effect

parameters.name: Mini-monopolies
parameters.signal: A monopoly-like position in the customer's mind or in aftermarket/services.
parameters.description: An unregulated monopoly gives the strongest profits and returns but gets targeted by governments. Mini-monopolies are about customer choices and exist in the customer's mind (e.g. brand preference), and in services the manufacturer holds a mini-monopoly on spare parts and software upgrades.
cautions: Overt (unregulated) monopolies attract government intervention

parameters.name: Partial monopoly / broken competition / switching costs
parameters.signal: Regional monopoly or captive aftermarket via switching costs.
parameters.description: Monopoly in some areas or countries (broken competition), and switching costs (razor-and-blade or software) where competition for the upfront product sale is intense but the aftermarket is captive.

parameters.name: Oligopoly (vs duopoly)
parameters.signal: Stable oligopoly; end customer lacks negotiating power.
parameters.description: An oligopoly is sometimes better than a duopoly - in a duopoly it can become an obsession to beat the other player. Prefer structures where the end customer has no negotiating power and where the industry structure has been stable for some time.
cautions: Duopolies can turn into destructive 'beat the rival' behaviour

parameters.name: Barriers to entry and rationality
parameters.signal: Few/no new entrants; rational pricing (no discount wars); stable ownership.
parameters.description: Distinguish barriers to entry (new players popping up) from barriers to success and scale. Look for industries with no or few new entrants; big firms still family-owned is a good sign of stability; companies should not engage in price cuts and pricing wars.
cautions: Price cuts / pricing wars and habitual discounting destroy industry economics

parameters.name: Share donators
parameters.signal: Presence of weak competitors from whom the target can take share.
parameters.description: Identify particular weak members in the industry who donate share. Most common sources: management incompetence, suboptimal products, ignored divisions of large companies, and smaller companies unable to scale.

parameters.name: Security by obscurity
parameters.signal: A humble, under-the-radar niche that competitors/capital ignore.
parameters.description: Businesses that keep out of sight of potential predators - important but humble corporate niches (locks, lenses, bathroom fittings) that financial and intellectual capital are not drawn towards.

parameters.name: Intangible benefits
parameters.signal: Pricing power from image/taste; steady demand; high gross margin.
parameters.description: Benefits that elude measurement - taste and image (high-end bags, cars, watches, jewelry). The smaller the ticket size, the bigger the role intangible benefits play. Consumers never test the comparative effects, so brand perception dominates.

parameters.name: Assurance benefits
parameters.signal: Customer buys certainty/reliability; price is secondary to trust.
parameters.description: Works where product reliability is of the utmost importance - the failure of a small component can shut down an entire plant, so customers pay for assurance and are price-insensitive.

parameters.name: Convenience benefits
parameters.signal: Superior accessibility and direct customer intimacy / strong sales force.
parameters.description: Making a product readily accessible, with customer intimacy - a direct relation with the customer, often via a strong sales force.

parameters.name: Customer types (retail vs corporate)
parameters.signal: Match benefit type to customer: intangibles for retail; TCO/reliability + switching-cost lock-in for corporate.
parameters.description: Retail customers are more willing to splurge on items with intangible benefits. Corporate clients do not pay for intangible benefits; they have departments that keep the purchase decision rational (total cost of ownership and reliability matter), and their switching costs are high and can therefore be exploited.

parameters.name: Technology advantage
parameters.signal: Deep, multi-product tech edge with high R&D intensity and superior customer benefit.
parameters.description: A competitive advantage derived through technology. It must NOT be a single product (single products get copied); the magnitude of the advantage must be large (not slight); percentage of R&D spend matters; it should deliver products with superior customer benefits. Includes incremental innovation and advantage in data collection and manipulation.
cautions: A single product will get copied; a slight advantage is not enough

parameters.name: Network effects
parameters.signal: Self-reinforcing two-sided network that strengthens with scale.
parameters.description: A system whose value increases as more people use it (more sellers -> more buyers and vice versa).
cautions: Too-strong network effects can backfire (UK housing agents formed a rival network)
A high pace of innovation is a risk (Facebook killed MySpace; killed MSN chat)

parameters.name: Distribution advantage
parameters.signal: A distribution/service reach rivals cannot match, especially where service is vital.
parameters.description: A route to consumers that is more effective than rivals'. When the company's ability to service or fix a product is vital to customers, distribution takes a critical role.
